“Does Allah Also Use Abusive Language?!!!” # The Misuse of Allah’s Words to Justify One’s Own Verbal Abuse: Not Merely a Serious Misconception, but an Outrageous Act of Presumption!

**1.**

In order to justify our own wrongdoing or portray an objectionable position of ours as being in conformity with the Sharīʿah, we, as ʿulamāʾ, sometimes resort to rather strange and illogical arguments. At times, we invoke the Prophets and Messengers (peace be upon them) in defence of our own conduct; at other times, we bring in the noble Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). By identifying superficial similarities between our own actions and something they said, did, or practised, we try to establish the legitimacy of our own position.

Yet, in such cases, we often fail to consider the actual significance, context, purpose, and the relevant Sharīʿah rulings associated with the words and actions of those Prophets, Messengers, or Companions. This is, on the one hand, a serious form of intellectual betrayal and, on the other, an attempt to distort the true significance of the statements and conduct of those revered personalities.

In several of my previous writings, I have drawn attention to such tendencies.

Recently, I came across an even more astonishing tendency on social media.

Some people, in an attempt to justify the abusive language and vulgar expressions used by their own *akābir* (senior religious figures), are now dragging Allah Almighty Himself into this controversy. Their argument is: **“But Allah also uses abusive language!”**

Such an argument is not merely an instance of false analogy or an illogical comparison. Rather, it reflects a grave failure to understand the true significance of Qur'anic statements and a tendency to misapply the rulings of the Sharīʿah. If someone deliberately distorts the actual meaning of Allah’s words in order to justify their own wrongdoing, this may even fall within the category of *taḥrīf maʿnawī*—distortion of meaning.

There is absolutely no justification for using any statement of Allah Almighty as a certificate of legitimacy for one’s objectionable behaviour or wrongful actions. This is not merely a serious intellectual and Sharīʿah-related misconception; it is also an extremely reprehensible and outrageous act of presumption.

**2.**

In the Holy Qur’an, Allah Almighty has condemned disbelievers, hypocrites, wrongdoers, and criminals; invoked His curse upon them; severely criticised their actions; and responded to their mockery and ridicule. However, there is no justification for equating these expressions with vulgar abusive language in the ordinary human sense.

When Allah Almighty condemns a wrongdoer, invokes a curse upon someone, or severely criticises an act of injustice, He does so on the basis of His perfect knowledge, wisdom, and justice. None of His statements can ever constitute injustice, obscenity, lack of restraint, or transgression of proper limits.

Human verbal abuse, on the other hand, may involve lies, slander, obscenity, hatred, personal animosity, and attacks on the honour of others.

Therefore, presenting Allah’s condemnation or curse of wrongdoers as evidence that human beings are entitled to engage in personal verbal abuse is a fundamental conceptual and Sharīʿah-related error.

One point needs to be acknowledged here:

In condemning wrongdoers and oppressors, the Holy Qur’an sometimes employs extremely stern and reproachful expressions. However, such expressions cannot be equated with obscene and vulgar abuse in the ordinary human sense. For rightly condemning a wrongdoer, exposing his moral degradation, and verbally abusing someone out of personal animosity are not the same thing.

Another important distinction should also be borne in mind.

Identifying errors in someone's opinions or actions, exposing the fallacy of their deviant beliefs or ideology, and criticising wrongdoing are not synonymous with verbal abuse. Refuting someone's errors through reason, evidence, and dignified language is entirely different from attacking them with obscene and degrading expressions.

**3.**

The guidance of the Holy Qur’an concerning verbal abuse and the use of indecent language is abundantly clear. Indeed, Muslims have even been prohibited from verbally abusing the objects of worship of others if doing so might provoke them into committing the grave offence of abusing Allah Almighty in retaliation!

Allah Almighty says:

**وَلَا تَسُبُّوا الَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ فَيَسُبُّوا اللَّهَ عَدْوًا بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ**

“Do not abuse those whom they invoke besides Allah, lest they, in hostility and without knowledge, abuse Allah.” — *Surah al-Anʿām, 6:108*

The significance of this verse is profound. On the one hand, it leaves intact the opportunity to expose the falsehood of other people's objects of worship and erroneous beliefs; on the other, it instructs Muslims to refrain from abusive language. This is because, while protesting against a false belief, it is not appropriate to adopt language or conduct that may lead to an even greater wrong and harm.

Therefore, there is no justification for conflating criticism of a deviant ideology, opposition to falsehood, and verbal abuse.

Similarly, while describing the linguistic and behavioural characteristics of a believer, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

**لَيْسَ الْمُؤْمِنُ بِالطَّعَّانِ وَلَا اللَّعَّانِ وَلَا الْفَاحِشِ وَلَا الْبَذِيءِ**

“A believer is neither one who constantly finds fault with others, nor one who frequently invokes curses, nor one who uses obscene or vulgar language.” — *Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī*

This hadith establishes an important standard for the moral character and linguistic propriety of a believer. In other words, although one has the right to stand for the truth and oppose wrongdoing, obscenity, vulgarity, and habitual verbal abuse cannot be regarded as desirable qualities of a believer.

**4.**

The statement “Allah also uses abusive language” may arise from two distinct tendencies or intentions. In light of the underlying meaning and the context in which the statement is used, both tendencies are reprehensible.

**A. Equating Allah’s condemnation, curses, and severe criticism with human verbal abuse.**

This reflects a failure to understand the true significance of Allah’s words and constitutes a serious conceptual and theological misconception. When Allah Almighty condemns a wrongdoer, invokes a curse upon someone, or severely criticises an act of injustice, it is an expression of His perfect knowledge, justice, and wisdom. There is no justification for treating such expressions as equivalent to obscene verbal abuse in the ordinary human sense.

**B. Using a statement of Allah as evidence to legitimise one’s own obscenity and verbal abuse.**

This is not merely a false comparison; rather, it is a misinterpretation of the Qur’anic message and a misapplication of the rulings of the Sharīʿah. The fact that Allah Almighty has condemned a wrongdoer or invoked His curse upon an oppressor does not establish the permissibility of obscene language and verbal abuse for human beings. The Sharīʿah ruling on an action is determined on the basis of its own evidence, purpose, nature, and context—not merely on the basis of a superficial resemblance to an action performed by someone else.

Thus, in the first case, the true significance of Allah’s words is being distorted; in the second, that distorted understanding is being used as a tool to legitimise one's own wrongful conduct. Both tendencies are utterly reprehensible.

**5.**

Islam does not prohibit criticising wrongdoing, opposing falsehood, condemning an oppressor, or demanding appropriate punishment for a criminal. On the contrary, establishing the truth, speaking out against injustice, and exposing the hollowness of falsehood are important teachings of Islam. However, resorting to obscenity, personal attacks, and verbal abuse is not a prerequisite for fulfilling these responsibilities.

One can speak the truth in stern language, refute an opponent’s errors through reason and evidence, and raise one's voice against injustice. But taking a stand for the truth does not confer upon anyone the right to cross the ethical boundaries of language.

Rather, a believer's speech should ideally combine truthfulness, civility, justice, and self-restraint.

**6.**

In short,

Allah Almighty has condemned wrongdoers, invoked His curse upon oppressors, and exposed the hollowness of falsehood in forceful language. But turning these statements into evidence to justify one's own verbal abuse is a grave logical fallacy.

Allah’s condemnation and curses are expressions of His perfect knowledge, wisdom, and justice; human verbal abuse, on the other hand, is often an expression of obscenity, ignorance, hatred, and moral weakness.

Therefore, attempting to legitimise one's own vulgarity through the words of Allah is not a proper application of the Qur’anic message. Rather, it is an attempt to use the Qur’an in support of one's own base desires.

One fundamental principle must be remembered here:

The fact that an action performed by a human being bears a superficial resemblance to an action of Allah does not mean that the Sharīʿah and moral rulings governing the two actions are identical. The permissibility of an action on the part of Allah and the permissibility of a seemingly similar action on the part of a human being are two entirely different matters.

Instead of making the words of Allah an excuse for following one's own desires, it is the responsibility of a believer to bring those desires under the guidance and command of Allah.
